The '''Pottawattamie County Jail''', also known as '''Squirrel Cage Jail''' in [[Council Bluffs, Iowa]], United States, was built in 1885 and it was listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] in 1972.<ref name="NRIS" />  The building is one of three extant "squirrel cage jails", also known as [[rotary jail]]s.  It was designated a [[National Historic Landmark]] in 2023.

==History==
Construction of the jail was simultaneous with that of the county's new courthouse, which was finished in 1888.<ref name="pottcounty">{{cite web|url=http://www.pottcounty.com/visitors/history.php |title=Pottawattamie County IA|publisher=Pottawattamie County, Iowa|access-date=2011-03-02|last= |first= }}</ref> It was designed by William H. Brown and Benjamin F. Haugh of [[Indianapolis, Indiana]],<ref name="pottcounty" /> at a cost of $30,000.<ref name="Historical Society">{{cite web|url=http://thehistoricalsociety.org/jail.htm|title=Historic Pottawattamie County Squirrel Cage Jail|publisher=Historical Society of Pottawattamie County|access-date=2011-03-02|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110308112949/http://thehistoricalsociety.org/jail.htm|archive-date=2011-03-08}}</ref>

The building was one of 18 such jails that were built in the United States and the only one that was three stories tall.<ref name="Historical Society" /> Also known as 'Squirrel Cage Jail', it was one of a handful of [[rotary jail]]s built in the Midwestern America in the mid-19th century. The building was designed for maximum security with minimal contact between the prisoners and the jailers.<ref name="pottcounty" /> The front part of the jail had offices for the jailer, a kitchen, trustee cells, and quarters for women. The rest of the building is made up of pie-shaped cells that revolved inside of a cage.

The building was used as a jail until its closure in 1969.<ref name="Historical Society" /> In 1971, the Council Bluffs Park Board acquired the building, and in 1977, the county historical society took ownership of the building and maintains it as a museum.

==In popular culture==
===Television===
The Pottawattamie County Jail was featured as a haunted location in a special episode of ''[[Ghost Adventures]]'' in 2019 titled, "Serial Killer Spirits: Axe-Killer Jail" which aired on the [[Travel Channel]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.travelchannel.com/shows/ghost-adventures/episodes/serial-killer-spirits-axe-killer-jail|title=Serial Killer Spirits: Axe Killer Jail}}</ref>

===Radio===
The jail was also referenced in an old time radio program [[Gang Busters]], in the episode Gang Busters – The Case of John K. Giles, which originally aired September 29, 1945.  In the episode [[John K. Giles]] is reportedly captured and sent to the "Pottawattamie Prison", a special jail with impregnable bars and microphones in the wall.  The escape artist fashioned a key out of a sharpened utensil and was able to unlock the cell door to get free.<ref>{{YouTube|id=t2vkinY_Q20|Gang Busters – The Case of John K. Giles|time=8m18s}}</ref>
